youtube.title: Taurid Meteor Shower: Where Do These Fireballs Come From?
youtube.description:
The Taurid meteor shower is not random space dust. Every October and November, Earth runs through the crumbs of Comet Encke, and some of them light up as big, slow Halloween fireballs.

Comet Encke loops the Sun every 3.3 years, the shortest orbit of any major comet, and it sheds rock on every lap. Johann Encke worked out its orbit in 1819 by showing that sightings from 1786, 1795, 1805 and 1818 were one comet. Most meteors are grains of sand, but Taurid pieces can be pebbles, so they burn longer and brighter. The North Taurids peak around November 12.

Subscribe to Stickstory for a true story like this every day. Have you ever seen a fireball? Tell me in the comments!

scenes.text: That fireball is a piece of a comet.
scenes.visual: Night on a hilltop above a small valley town with lit windows: the fez host stands big, pointing up in surprise, then jumps back in shock; one huge slow fireball with a gold-red tapering trail and sparks streaks across the starry sky right over him; dark grass and rocks in the foreground.

scenes.text: Every November, the Taurids send big, slow fireballs overhead.
scenes.visual: Over town rooftops at night: rows of dark roofs with chimneys, smoke and gold windows fill the lower two thirds; two slow fireballs cross the starry sky one after the other; serif card 'NOVEMBER'.

A full-frame hand-drawn orbit chart: the Sun with turning gold rays near the top, dashed orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, a ring of asteroid dots; a long red dashed ellipse draws itself, and a big comet with a rocky nucleus, glowing coma and two tails sits on it near the Sun; red card 'COMET ENCKE'.

scenes.text: named for Johann Encke, who cracked its orbit.
scenes.visual: A study in 1819 by candlelight: a hatless astronomer in a dark coat writes with a quill at a wooden desk; four pinned notes on the wall each show a small comet and a year (1786, 1795, 1805, 1818); on 'cracked' a red thread joins them into one arc, on 'orbit' an ellipse is sketched on his sheet; hand label 'Johann Encke'.

scenes.text: It loops the Sun every 3.3 years,
scenes.visual: The orbit chart again: the comet races one full lap of its long red ellipse, whipping fast past the Sun and crawling far out near the asteroid ring, its tail always pointing away from the Sun; a big red serif card '3.3 YEARS' pops in.

Close-up on the inner orbit chart: as the comet swings past the Sun it leaves a trail of rocky crumbs along its red ellipse, and soon crumbs lie all around the orbit; little blue Earth runs into them with red sparks.

scenes.text: A normal meteor is a grain of sand.
scenes.visual: A night study table under a window: a big magnifying glass hovers over a single sand grain in a small dish and shows it big; through the window thin faint shooting stars flick past; a red dashed arrow runs from the grain up to the window; red card 'SAND GRAIN'.

scenes.text: But Taurid pieces can be pebbles, so they burn longer and brighter.
scenes.visual: Two meteors over dark pine hills at night: under the blue 'SAND' card thin fast meteors flick and die at once, one after another; on 'pebbles' a fat bright fireball on the right burns a long way down, flares and leaves a smoky train ('PEBBLE').

scenes.text: See one this week? You're watching a comet fall apart.
scenes.visual: From behind a row of watchers in beanies, brimmed hats and hoods on a dark hill (heads and shoulders fill the bottom), the middle one raises an arm and points up as a slow fireball crosses the sky over the valley town and its pines; a faint ghost comet with its tail hangs high in the sky.

scenes.text: Subscribe for a true story like this every day.
scenes.visual: Close-up over the town rooftops: the fez host's face fills the frame, pointing up in wonder while glowing gold comet crumbs drift down around him past chimney smoke; then he turns to the viewer and waves.
